title: Update on my falling sand voxel project
author: Synyster328
selftext:
Using Codex CLI on Windows, I thought "What if I modify the Godot engine's source code to facilitate custom voxel shapes and physics?"

Here's a small sample after a few days of tinkering. I made a post a few days ago of some other voxel simulations, but I wasn't happy with the performance and movements of the cube voxels, so I went down this rabbit hole and I'm pretty happy with the way it's turning out. Not without my share of frustrating 3am hallucination-fueled AI pair-programming moments, that's for sure, but with some patience the progress is slow and steady.

comments.author: aiwithphil
comments.body: Hey that's pretty cool! How many grains of sand and what FPS? What are the limits and sweet points?

replies.author: Synyster328
replies.body:
I thought about writing this myself, but in the spirit of the sub, here's what Codex responded with:

Right now it’s a small hourglass test on a BCC lattice. On my Windows box (RTX 4090, custom Godot build, VSync off), the default 24³ grid spawns \~127 sand voxels. Scaling up: a 128³ grid gives \~52.5k grains, and 256³ gives \~462k grains.

FPS is mostly driven by render resolution. At 512×512:



\- 128³ grid: \~168 FPS

\- 160³ grid: \~173 FPS

\- 256³ grid: \~138 FPS



Pushing the same 256³ grid with higher resolution:



\- 1024×1024: \~127 FPS

\- 1536×1536: \~51 FPS

\- 2048×2048: \~39 FPS

\- 3072×3072: \~18 FPS



Sweet spot for me is 512×512 with a 128–160 grid (50k–100k grains) at \~170–180 FPS. Limits start to show up when I crank resolution to 2–3K or go beyond a 256 grid. With VSync on it just caps to monitor refresh.

\---

Thanks for asking by the way, I hadn't gotten around to actually benchmarking yet so this was a fun exercise. I couldn't believe it actually went as high as it did, it was fucking massive while still going smooth as butter.

replies.author: aiwithphil
replies.body:
Those are actually impressive stats. Very cool. Thank you for sharing!


Will this algorithm be able to handle liquid instead of sand?

replies.author: Synyster328
replies.body: For sure, that's what I'm planning to do once the engine gets a bit more stable. I was inspired by projects like John Lin's Sandbox, Sandboxels, and Teardown. The rules are fairly straightforward, the hardest parts of optimizing on the GPU and doing the custom shapes is already done. I definitely was not expecting that it would be able to handle such high counts of grains. Before the optimizations, when it was still involving the CPU to track the states and interactions, I was lucky to have a few hundred voxels actively simulating at a time without grinding FPS to a halt.

replies.author: aiwithphil
replies.body:
Teardown is amazing in terms of performance and the technology achievements there..


However you know it's limitations and looks like you're trying to solve it. Awesome. 


Nvidia released a lot of white papers on different techniques to use for crunching these kind of numbers. I would take one of those papers and ask Claude code to analyze it, analyze your code, and come up with optimizations based on those techniques

replies.author: Synyster328
replies.body: Oh nice, thanks for the tip. Do you know the names of any of those papers I can check out as a starting point?
